rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
R_x = Σ F cosθ
R_y = Σ F sinθ
R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: You cannot add the magnitudes of vectors that point in different directions.  ·  tanα needs the quadrant. A calculator's arctan may sit in the wrong one.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Three forces in equilibrium have R_x = 0 and R_y = 0.  ·  Keep one pair of axes for the whole sum.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: When several vectors lie in one plane, resolve each one into x and y components, then add the components separately. Components along the same line add as ordinary signed numbers.  ·  R_x is the sum of every F cosθ, with a minus sign if that component points along the negative axis. R_y is the sum of every F sinθ, with the same care about signs.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Summing F cosθ and then also adding the original F double-counts.  ·  Opposite components cancel before the square root is taken.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: The resultant magnitude is sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2). The angle with the +x-axis satisfies tanα = |R_y / R_x|, and the quadrant follows the signs of R_x and R_y.  ·  This component method is the working form of the polygon law. Drawing the polygon is the picture. Adding components is the calculation.  ·  A vector along the negative x-axis has F_x = −F and F_y = 0. A vector straight down has F_x = 0 and F_y = −F. Leaving these signs out is the usual arithmetic error.
